weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q65. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]].
stem: Which of the following is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)?

options.html: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT.

answer: The correct answer is E. All of the above are relative contraindications, but no absolute contraindications to ECT exist. ECT is a safe and effective management option for depression — a point the workbook makes again in Q77 for the elderly.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q65. Tests [[06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants]].
stem: Which of the following would be appropriate counselling for a patient regarding starting an MAOI?

options.html: Patients should avoid eating aged cheeses or preserved foods as this may precipitate serotonin syndrome.
Concurrent use of Imitrex (sumatriptan) may precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
Patients can switch between antidepressants by gradually decreasing the dose of their SSRI antidepressant while simultaneously increasing their dose of an MAOI.
The mechanism of the interaction between MAOIs and aged/pickled/smoked foods involves tyramine metabolism.
MAOIs are an appropriate first line treatment for children and adolescents with severe depression.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Aged cheeses and pickled/smoked foods contain tyramine, which cannot be metabolized in the presence of MAOIs and leads to a hypertensive crisis by increasing NE activity.

A and B are the same two facts with their consequences swapped: the food interaction causes a hypertensive crisis (not serotonin syndrome, killing A), while sumatriptan is serotonergic and could precipitate serotonin syndrome (not a hypertensive crisis, killing B).

C is dangerous: MAOIs must not be given concurrently with any other serotonergic antidepressant — there must be a "wash out" period, recommended 2 weeks. E is wrong because although effective, MAOIs are not first line for depression/anxiety and are not usually given to children because of their side effect profile.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q25. Tests [[08 - Suicide]].
stem: Ms. Edwards is a 35-year-old woman who was admitted to the hospital after her most recent suicide attempt. Her husband came home early from his camping trip and found her unconscious in the garage with the car turned on. This is not Ms. Edwards' first time attempting suicide. 2 years ago she took a bunch of pills but her husband found the empty bottles and she was rushed to the hospital and treated. When speaking with her about what happened she mentions that she wished her husband hadn't found her and that she would consider trying again. When prompted she mentions different ways of committing suicide but doesn't seem to have settled on anything or have a concrete plan. What factor makes her most at risk for committing suicide over the next 5 years?

options.html: The fact that her method of previous attempts had a high lethality
The fact that this is her second time attempting suicide
The fact that she has a vague idea of how she would attempt suicide again
The fact that she is female
The fact that she is over 30

answer:
The correct answer is A. When previous attempts have had high lethality, individuals are more likely to have completed suicide at 5-year follow-up. Carbon monoxide poisoning in a closed garage is a high-lethality method.

The other options are all genuine considerations that are simply weaker predictors than lethality of method — and note D is the wrong direction: female sex is associated with more attempts but lower completion.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Anais is a ten-year-old girl who you have diagnosed with clinical depression. Her mother also has clinical depression and tells you that she is confused by your diagnosis, since Anais' mood does not at all resemble what the mother experiences when she is depressed. Which of the following is TRUE regarding the differences between depression in children and in adults?

options.html: Anais would be less likely to experience irritability and anxiety than an adult.
Pretend play that centers on death and dying is the equivalent of Anais' mother saying that she wants to commit suicide.
It would not be concerning if Anais were to maintain her present weight for an extended period of time.
If Anais were to hear voices or see things, this would automatically be a sign of a severe depression.
If Anais had had subthreshold symptoms of depression for a year, this would not meet criteria for dysthymia.

answer:
The correct answer is B. Four developmental differences, each correcting one option:

  • Children tend to experience greater irritability (and anxiety) — kills A
  • They may fail to reach expected weight gains rather than losing weight — so a child holding a static weight is concerning, killing C
  • They may report psychotic-like experiences even in the context of mild depression — so hallucinations are not automatically a marker of severity, killing D
  • Dysthymia may be diagnosed after 1 year in children (versus 2 years in adults) — killing E
  • Children may express suicidal ideation as death-related play ✓

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Anais' mother asks you what treatment is the most likely to help Anais feel better. What do you tell her?

options.html: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) is a safe and effective treatment for young children with depression.
The only first line pharmacological treatment for depression in children is Cipralex (escitalopram).
Combining cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) with an SSRI does not provide any additional benefit in children with severe depressive symptoms.
If Anais' depression is treated with cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), her mother can expect her therapy to last for 1-2 years.
If Anais is started on an SSRI, she would be given an adult dose.

answer:
The correct answer is E. SSRIs are not dosed by age or weight — a child receives an adult dose.

The rest of the treatment picture:

  • Options for children are SSRI medication and CBT. IPT may be used in adolescents, but not in children — kills A
  • The only first-line SSRI is fluoxetine (Prozac) — all others are second line, killing B
  • The optimal treatment for severe depression is CBT combined with medication — killing C
  • CBT is a short-term therapy which can last as little as 6-12 weeks, with possible "booster" sessions afterwards — killing D

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Janice goes to see a therapist because of her severe social anxiety and obsessive compulsive disorder. Which of the following is MOST LIKELY to be true?

options.html: A cognitive therapist would ask Janice to write down the thoughts that she has about how people are evaluating her in social situations, and attempt to challenge those thoughts.
A therapist practicing ERP (a subtype of CBT) would ask Janice to approach a situation that she fears without engaging in a ritual for a maximum of five minutes.
A behavioural therapist would focus on how Janice's actions reflect experiences from her past.
A psychodynamic psychiatrist would not be interested in details of Janice's childhood and developmental history.
A therapist practicing IPT would not explicitly process Janice's feelings about termination, as IPT does not usually work with transference.

answer:
The correct answer is A. The modality map:

  • A cognitive therapist focuses on modifying problematic cognitions that impair function ✓
  • A behavioural therapist focuses on modifying behaviour in the present — so C (past experiences) is describing psychodynamic work
  • In Exposure and Response Prevention, the patient remains in the situation until her anxiety subsides, without performing any rituals — so B's "maximum of five minutes" is wrong; the endpoint is habituation, not the clock (compare Q4's "Prolonged")
  • A psychodynamic psychiatrist would focus on the impact of childhood experiences and conflicts — killing D

flags.title: Name inconsistency
flags.html: The stem introduces "Janice" but the options and the key alternate between Janice and Janet (and Q73-74's key refers to Janet). Same patient.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a potential area of focus for IPT?
answer: The correct answer is E — social isolation. The four IPT focus areas are grief, role transition, interpersonal conflict and interpersonal deficit. Social isolation is a consequence that IPT may address, not one of its named problem areas.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter and the phrase only.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q70-Q74. Tests [[10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is similar across therapeutic modalities as practiced in the community?

options.html: Strict adherence to a single approach

answer:
The correct answer is A. Resistance is normal and expected in all types of therapy, and is not always under the patient's conscious control.

Therapies vary in their use of transference, adherence to goal setting, and frequency of meetings — killing B, C and D. And E is the opposite of practice: while community therapists may have an area of focus, it is most common to practice an eclectic-integrative approach focused on the needs of the client.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q78-Q79. Tests [[11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses]].
stem: Common comorbidities that occur with chronic pain include all but?
answer:
The correct answer is E. The real comorbidity rates in chronic pain:

  • Depression occurs in 8-50%
  • Anxiety as a symptom occurs in 50%; an anxiety disorder in 19-30%
  • Substance misuse — higher than the general population
  • Anger — many report it

Psychosis is not on the list.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q78-Q79. Tests [[11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses]].
stem: Brenda is a 19-year-old woman who is currently undergoing treatment for breast cancer, and presents to you with concerns about her mood. Her appetite is decreased, she has no desire to see her friends, and she cries for most of the day. She does not sleep well and complains of initial insomnia as well as frequent awakenings. You wonder if you should prescribe an SSRI to help with her symptoms. Which of the following is TRUE about management of Brenda's condition?

options.html: The majority of patients with a medical illness will meet criteria for major depression at some point during their illness.
You will need to rule out adjustment disorder, since supportive psychotherapy would be superior to an SSRI for that diagnosis.
Because of Brenda's medical condition, SSRI medications should be given at a lower dose than a healthy adult would receive.
Paxil (paroxetine) would be the best choice of SSRI for a woman receiving tamoxifen.
If Brenda is treated with an SSRI, psychotherapy will likely not be necessary.

answer:
The correct answer is B. If the diagnosis were adjustment disorder, supportive psychotherapy would be superior to an SSRI — so it must be ruled out first.

Each distractor:

  • A — fewer than 30% of patients with a medical illness meet criteria for depression
  • C — SSRIs should still be given at the normal dose
  • D — Paxil decreases blood levels of tamoxifen and would be a poor choice in a breast cancer patient
  • E — psychotherapy may be useful as an adjunct

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q13, Q78-Q79. Tests [[11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses]].
stem: You initiate therapy with Cipralex (escitalopram), and Brenda's symptoms improve. You continue to follow her over the course of treatment for her cancer. Which of the following is TRUE about Brenda's experience?

options.html: The successful treatment of her depression has the potential to improve her prognosis.
As Brenda's treatment nears an end, you can expect her to experience a sense of relief and improvement in her mood.
Her age and gender put her in a lower risk bracket for developing depression as a result of medical illness.
Brenda's desire to conquer her illness will likely prevent her from considering suicide.
Brenda's depression is likely psychological and does not have a physiological basis.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Successful treatment of depression has the potential to improve the prognosis of the medical illness itself.

B is the counterintuitive point worth keeping: high-risk times for depression include at the point of diagnosis and at the completion of treatment, as social support may decrease and patients must emerge from "survival mode" and begin to reorganize their lives. So the end of treatment is a risk period, not a relief.

weekLabel: Week 17 - Mood Disorders, Antidepressants, Suicide & the Mental Status Exam
lectureMeta: Workbook Q58. Tests [[12 - Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages]].
stem: Beverly tells you that she is considering becoming pregnant, and wants to know if there is an SSRI that pregnant women can take safely. Of the SSRIs, you tell her that __________ carries a risk of serious birth defects, and that __________ is considered to be comparatively safe.
answer: The correct answer is A. Paxil (paroxetine) carries a risk of serious birth defects; Prozac (fluoxetine) is considered comparatively safe.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. Note that paroxetine is the problem drug in three consecutive questions — worst withdrawal (Q51, Q57), teratogenicity (Q58) — which is a reasonable way to remember it.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: A person with Social anxiety disorder (SAD) will finish this statement: When I am in a crowd of people, I worry that…

options.html: I will get contaminated with everyone's germs
I will do something embarrassing and everyone will look at me and laugh
I will feel closed in and panicky
I will run into a clown

answer:
The correct answer is B. People with SAD worry about being judged and about embarrassing themselves, especially in social situations.

The distractors are the same crowd from four other diagnoses' points of view: A is OCD (contamination), C is paranoia, D is panic disorder/agoraphobia, E is a specific phobia.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Blood/injection/injury type phobias differ from other phobia subtypes in that:

options.html: They cause a decrease in blood pressure
Applied muscle tension does not work

answer:
The correct answer is A. Blood/injection/injury phobias cause a decrease in blood pressure — a vasovagal response — whereas other phobias produce sympathetic arousal with a rise in BP.

That physiology is also why applied muscle tension is the specific treatment for this subtype (making D false).

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the five types of specific phobias?

options.html: Natural Environment, Animals, Insects, Situational, Blood/injection/injury
Blood/injection/injury, Animals, Natural Environment, Situational, Other
Blood/injection/injury, Situational, Food, Natural Environment, Other

answer: The correct answer is C — Blood/injection/injury, Animals, Natural Environment, Situational, Other. See specific phobia.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The discriminators across the options: "Situational" and "Other" must both be present, and "Food", "People", "Places" and "Insects" are not subtypes.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Meg is a 25-year-old woman who comes to your office complaining about persistent anxiety. She tells you that she constantly worries about the future and thinks about everything that could possibly go wrong with her job, her health, and her finances. She often needs to call her husband during the day to "check" that he is still alive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for Meg?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Meg exhibits worries about a wide variety of life events, which interfere with her function — the definition of GAD.

The trap is the checking behaviour: patients with GAD may engage in "checking" behaviour despite not having OCD. Checking alone does not make it OCD — the obsession/compulsion structure of Q14 is what would.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Meg asks you to help her understand whether cognitive behavioural therapy or medication is the best treatment for her. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice to give Meg?

options.html: Cognitive behavioural therapy is just as effective as medication – she should choose whichever she prefers.
Combining cognitive behavioural therapy with medication increases Meg's chances of remission.
Benzodiazepines would be the first line medication for Meg's condition.
If Meg chooses cognitive behavioural therapy, it will likely take at least a year for her to see results.
If Meg chooses treatment with medication, she can expect to continue taking it for the rest of her life.

answer:
The correct answer is A. CBT with medication is no better than either alone, but they have equal efficacy — so the choice can be made on patient preference. That equality is also what makes B false.

  • C — first line is an SSRI, or CBT; benzodiazepines are not first line
  • D — CBT is a short-term psychotherapy
  • E — medication should be continued for at least a year, after which the patient may try to discontinue, though 20-40% will relapse within a year of discontinuation

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Hilary's family is taking a vacation to Brazil, which they have been planning for the past year. Hilary wants to go, but she feels that she cannot because of her fear of snakes. She worries that she will suddenly encounter a snake and feels that if she did, she would not be able to handle it. Which of the following is TRUE about the treatment of Hilary's phobia?

options.html: It could involve carrying a rubber snake in her purse.
On the first day of treatment, Hilary would be asked to hold a boa constrictor.
If Hilary became too upset during the session, she would be encouraged to leave the room until she could calm down.
The therapist would likely use the exact same exposures for every person with a phobia of snakes.
It would likely take years for Hilary to improve enough to go to Brazil.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Four principles of exposure therapy for a specific phobia:

  • A hierarchy of exposures is used, beginning with something less fearful — such as thinking about the word "snake" — so B (a boa constrictor on day one) is wrong, and carrying a rubber snake is a plausible mid-hierarchy step ✓
  • The patient is expected to remain in the situation until her anxiety decreases — so C (leaving to calm down) defeats the mechanism
  • The hierarchy is constructed based on the individual's specific fears and thoughts — killing D
  • Exposure therapy is very effective and can show results relatively quickly — killing E

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Mallory is a young woman who presents to your office complaining of sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and a choking sensation in her throat. When this occurs, she feels scared that she is having a heart attack and will often go to the emergency department. Despite multiple tests, she feels sure that she has a heart condition and is no longer willing to leave her house because of concerns that she will have an attack and not be able to get help. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Two diagnoses stacked:

  • Sudden onset of untriggered symptoms of panic leading to concern about having another attack is diagnostic of panic disorder (4+ symptoms out of 13)
  • Her fear of situations where she would not be able to get help in the event of an attack is diagnostic of agoraphobia — this is the specific definition, not simply "fear of leaving the house"

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: You decide to treat Mallory with medication to help her symptoms and improve her functioning. Which of the following is TRUE about your treatment approach?

options.html: Treatment should continue until Mallory is able to leave her house again, even if she no longer has panic attacks.
Mallory would not need adjunctive Klonopin (clonazepam) due to how quickly antidepressants begin to work.
Medication should never be continued for longer than one year.
Anafranil (clomipramine) would be a first line medication for Mallory's condition.
Mallory should continue to go to the emergency department when she has an attack, just in case she does have an underlying heart condition.

answer:
The correct answer is A. First-line medication is an SSRI, continued for one year from the time when the agoraphobia — not the panic attacks — remits, and potentially longer depending on the situation. That is exactly what A says, and it also makes C wrong.

  • B is backwards: SSRIs take 6-12 weeks to work, so Klonopin could be considered to bridge the gap
  • D — clomipramine is a TCA and not first line here
  • E — patients should be educated that they are not dying or seriously medically ill, and should not go to the ED

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Maria is a 26-year-old university student who comes to you because of difficulties with attending lectures, which have led to severe academic difficulties. She tells you that when she is about to enter the classroom, she begins to feel shaky and sweaty, and her heart starts to pound. Sometimes she wonders if she is about to die. She worries that people in class are staring at her. Her worries make her feel very uncomfortable and then she begins to worry that others are noticing how uncomfortable she is and thinking that she is strange. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. Patients with social anxiety disorder may experience panic attacks, but they are triggered by social situations — versus untriggered in panic disorder (compare Q84). Anxiety about being evaluated negatively, confined to social situations, is diagnostic of social anxiety disorder.

flags.title: Two different patients named Maria
flags.html: The case vignette that follows this question (and drives Q88-89) is about a completely different Maria — a woman in a cocktail dress picked up by police. This Maria, the university student, has nothing to do with those two questions.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Which of the following anxiety disorders do you suspect in a 27-year-old female presenting with recurrent and persistent episodes of excessive worry and fear about a variety of things, along with restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Per the DSM-5, GAD is excessive anxiety and worry about a variety of events or activities, lasting at least six months, and difficult to control, plus at least three of:

  • restlessness
  • fatigue
  • difficulty concentrating
  • irritability
  • muscle tension
  • sleep disturbance

The stem gives five of the six.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q21, Q23, Q81-Q85, Q87, Q91-Q92. Tests [[01 - Anxiety Disorders]], [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Continuation of question 91: What additional information would you need to make a definitive diagnosis?

options.html: Her family history of mental illness
The severity and frequency of her symptoms
Her use of alcohol and other substances

answer: The correct answer is C. Information about symptom severity and frequency is needed to assess the severity of the disorder and the level of functional impairment. Further evaluation of medical and psychiatric history may also be necessary to rule out other potential causes.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q4. Tests [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: Interoceptive exposures are most commonly used to treat which of the following?
answer: The correct answer is A. Interoceptive exposures are exposures to a physical sensation or symptom that leads to anxiety. They are particularly effective in panic disorder, because it is the fear of the physical symptoms elicited by a panic attack that drives panic disorder — so the exposure has to be to the sensation itself, not to a situation.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q4. Tests [[03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD]].
stem: When implementing the 5 P's of CBT exposure therapy, which of the following is not part of the treatment protocol?
answer: The correct answer is B. Exposures need to be practiced frequently for habituation to occur — without that, the person never experiences the full decline in their anxiety levels. So the 5 P's are Planned, Practiced (frequently), Prolonged, Predictable, Paced. See cognitive behavioral therapy.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q12, Q14. Tests [[02 - Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder]].
stem: Ms. Brown is a 25-year-old woman who comes into your office today complaining about how her nose is much too large for her face, though from your point of view her nose is not large at all. Every time you try to ask about other complaints and symptoms she keeps talking about her nose and how horrible it is. She brings up the topic of surgery and asks you what you think. What is she suffering from?
answer:
The correct answer is D. body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with an imagined defect, or the exaggeration of a mild anomaly — and they often seek surgery, which is the tell in this stem.

The neighbours: somatization disorder, conversion disorder and somatoform pain disorder all involve pain or other physical symptoms that don't correlate with a detected disease. Hypochondriasis is preoccupation with having a serious disease — a disease, not a defect.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q12, Q14. Tests [[02 - Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder]].
stem: Which of the following examples best describes Obsessions and Compulsions associated with OCD?

options.html: Marie obsesses about her grades, and she is aiming for a 4.0 GPA. Her marks are always on the forefront of her mind. She always feels compelled to take at least 10 sharpened pencils with her to every exam, in case her pencils break.

John has intrusive thoughts about his mother's death that are extremely distressing for him. He believes that his mother will remain safe as long as he remembers to say her full name out loud exactly 7 times before leaving his house. Repeating her name alleviates the distress associated with her potential death.

Phil has an obsession with rainbows. He organizes his closet by color so that it looks like a rainbow, and even arranges the foods in his fridge by color. When something is out of place, he becomes very frustrated because it takes him much longer to find what he needs.

Damian is obsessed with car license plates and likes to read the plate of every car he passes on his way to work. He says that whenever he is in a rush and misses too many, he ends up having a worse day.
Ted has developed an obsession with online shopping. He feels compelled to buy a new outfit each time he has a bad day at work.

answer:
The correct answer is B. The definitions:

  • Obsessions are recurrent, inappropriate, intrusive, distressing thoughts / impulses / images
  • Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts the individual feels drawn to perform in order to reduce distress or prevent a feared outcome

The difference that decides this question: obsessions are egodystonic and increase anxiety; compulsions are egosyntonic and reduce anxiety. Only B has both halves — an intrusive, distressing thought plus a ritual that alleviates the distress. The others describe preferences, superstitions or impulses the person is not distressed by. See obsessive compulsive disorder.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q10, Q66-Q69. Tests [[05 - Personality Disorders]]. Q66-Q67 are one case (Pierre); the "Bill" of Q43-Q44 in the ADHD section is never introduced by the workbook.
stem: A 45-year-old lawyer seeking treatment. His wife was unhappy with their marriage, tired of his stubborn, perfectionist ways. In terms of his work, he was the youngest full partner in his firm's history, famous for handling many cases at the same time. He would not turn down a new case, and was never satisfied with the quality of work performed. He was never satisfied by the work done by his staff, to the point where he found himself constantly correcting and redoing their briefs and written documents. He has always been this way. What is your diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. OCPD is a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control at the expense of flexibility, with preoccupation with details, rules, lists, order, organization or schedules.

The OCD/OCPD distinction, which the workbook makes twice (see also Q66-67):

  • OCD is focused on particular distressing obsessions — repeated handwashing, abnormal fears of danger. Perfection for them is a sterile, danger-free environment.
  • OCPD is a broader approach — a constant mindset of order and compulsion.
  • The key discriminator: the OCPD person is not distressed by their condition; the OCD person is disturbed by their abnormal thoughts and actions. "He has always been this way" is the personality-disorder cue.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q10, Q66-Q69. Tests [[05 - Personality Disorders]]. Q66-Q67 are one case (Pierre); the "Bill" of Q43-Q44 in the ADHD section is never introduced by the workbook.
stem: Pierre is a 47-year-old male who lives with his wife and son. His wife brings him to your office complaining that he is "making her miserable". He refuses to allow anyone else to do household tasks, such as washing dishes, because they "don't do it right". If someone does wash a dish, Pierre must wash it again to make sure it is really clean. He has few friends and frequently volunteers to work long hours at his job so that he can save more money, rather than spend time with his family. When you ask Pierre about this, he says that he does not have a problem and that really it is everyone else who doesn't know how to do things the right way. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis for Pierre?
answer:
The correct answer is B — OCPD. Pierre exhibits preoccupation with orderliness, a pervasive pattern of perfectionism, miserliness, and excessive devotion to work and productivity.

The line "he does not have a problem and really it is everyone else" is the discriminator — see Q67 and compare Q10.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q10, Q66-Q69. Tests [[05 - Personality Disorders]]. Q66-Q67 are one case (Pierre); the "Bill" of Q43-Q44 in the ADHD section is never introduced by the workbook.
stem: Which of the following is TRUE about Pierre's presentation?

options.html: Pierre's symptoms, as he describes them, are ego dystonic (ego alien).
Pierre does not have a personality disorder because he does not believe there is anything odd about his behaviour.
Pierre's most likely diagnosis is a Cluster A personality disorder.
Pierre's symptoms likely began suddenly within the past decade, due to an identifiable life stressor.
While medication or CBT may be able to help Pierre function better socially, it is unlikely that treatment will alter his core personality pathology.

answer:
The correct answer is E. Treatment for personality disorders other than BPD is currently quite poor; while symptoms may improve, the likelihood of a cure is low. The focus of treatment is generally on improving functioning and relationships.

Each distractor corrected:

  • A — Pierre's symptoms are ego syntonic, because he does not experience them as intrusive or disturbing — which is typical for a personality disorder (and is exactly why B is backwards)
  • B — the lack of insight is characteristic of, not incompatible with, a personality disorder
  • C — OCPD is a cluster C (anxious/fearful) disorder, not cluster A
  • D — symptoms of a personality disorder must be traceable to adolescence or early adulthood, not to a recent stressor

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q10, Q66-Q69. Tests [[05 - Personality Disorders]]. Q66-Q67 are one case (Pierre); the "Bill" of Q43-Q44 in the ADHD section is never introduced by the workbook.
stem: Jessica is a 25-year-old graduate student who presents to the Emergency Department with numerous shallow lacerations on her wrists and upper arms. She tells you that ever since her therapist left for a week-long vacation, she has been unable to sleep and has felt extremely agitated and unhappy, so she cut herself with a razor blade to help her calm down. She is very angry that her therapist is gone and tells you that she plans to quit therapy because she can't trust someone who is willing to abandon her by going on vacation. Which of the following is TRUE about Jessica?

options.html: The condition which Jessica likely has is highly amenable to targeted psychotherapy.
Jessica's mood swings suggest that she likely has bipolar disorder and she should be started on lithium immediately.
You should send Jessica home without speaking to her, as she is probably just looking for attention.
This is a high lethality suicide attempt and she should be put on a Form 1 immediately.
Jessica's excessive reliance on her therapist suggests that dependent personality disorder is the most likely diagnosis.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Jessica's extreme fear of abandonment, combined with her difficulty coping with her emotions and her anger, suggest borderline personality disorder — and BPD is the one personality disorder that is highly amenable to targeted psychotherapy (contrast Q67E).

The differentials and the clinical points:

  • E — a patient with DPD would respond with appeasement rather than anger and dysregulation
  • B — these rapid mood swings are characteristic of BPD rather than bipolar disorder, which occurs over a longer time course
  • D — many patients with BPD engage in deliberate self-harm and, while there is a high risk of suicide, repeated hospitalizations can be regressive and should be avoided where possible
  • C — patients with BPD should be treated with respect and kindness in emergency settings, as they are often in extreme distress

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q10, Q66-Q69. Tests [[05 - Personality Disorders]]. Q66-Q67 are one case (Pierre); the "Bill" of Q43-Q44 in the ADHD section is never introduced by the workbook.
stem: Ryan is a 26-year-old male who is brought to your office by his mother, who has concerns about his behaviour. She tells you that he has few close friends, and does not seem interested in forming friendships. He has never had a sexual or romantic relationship and does not seem to desire one. In your office, his face is difficult to read and he does not express emotion. He tells you that he prefers to spend his time alone, playing video games or painting. You are concerned that Ryan has a cluster A personality disorder. Which of the following would support the diagnosis of SCHIZOID personality disorder as opposed to schizotypal personality disorder?

options.html: Ryan does not desire intimate relationships or friendships.
Ryan's affect in your office appears flat.
Ryan has never had any psychotic or quasi-psychotic experiences.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Both schizoid and schizotypal personality disorder involve a preference for solitary activities, few close relationships, and constricted or flat affect — which is why A, B and E cannot discriminate.

What separates them: schizotypal patients also exhibit quasi-psychotic experiences and social anxiety; schizoid patients do not. So the absence of psychotic-like experiences (D) supports schizoid — and C, if present, would point the other way.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11. Tests [[06 - Dissociation and Dissociative Disorders]].
stem: Jane Doe was found wandering around downtown London and brought into the hospital by the police. They find her wallet and look at the license and it says she is from Montreal. She has no recollection how she got here and is not able to answer any questions about her past or who she is. What dissociative disorder is she suffering from?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A dissociative fugue is characterized by sudden, unexpected travel away from home, accompanied by inability to recall one's past and confusion about personal identity, or the assumption of a new identity.

The travel is what separates it from dissociative amnesia — Montreal to London is the detail that makes it a fugue.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q42-Q44. Tests [[07 - Approach to ADHD]].
stem: Which of the following is TRUE about ADHD?

options.html: The prevalence of ADHD is much higher in Canada and the USA than anywhere else in the world, because ADHD is a "fake" disease invented by doctors and pharmaceutical companies.
Patients with ADHD generally outgrow it by adulthood.
ADHD only affects school performance, so it is okay if parents want to only give ADHD medications on school days.
A PET scan of a person with ADHD would be expected to show increased cerebral metabolism in the prefrontal cortex.
ADHD can first come to medical attention later in life, as people who are very intelligent or have excellent environmental support may be able to compensate in earlier years.

answer:
The correct answer is E. ADHD can first come to medical attention later in life, because people who are very intelligent or have excellent environmental support may compensate in earlier years.

The distractors: ADHD is not outgrown by most (B); it affects far more than school performance, so medication holidays limited to weekends are not automatically appropriate (C); and PET would show decreased, not increased, prefrontal metabolism (D).

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q42-Q44. Tests [[07 - Approach to ADHD]].
stem: How would you counsel Bill's parents regarding behavioural management of his ADHD?

options.html: It is okay if parents and teachers do not coordinate their approaches, as long as the expectations are appropriate.
The best way to motivate a child with ADHD is to encourage them to have pride in their accomplishments, rather than using external rewards.
Children with ADHD respond well to verbal discussions about the importance of paying attention.
If Bill is able to concentrate for extended periods when he is playing video games, his parents should bring him back for re-evaluation.
Bill's teacher should be flexible with Bill by allowing him to fidget in class, or to listen to music while doing individual work.

answer:
The correct answer is E. Allowing for some hyperactivity in the classroom is very helpful. The four principles behind the other options:

  • Children with ADHD require a consistent approach from all involved — kills A
  • They often require external, highly salient rewards, as well as externalization of time — kills B
  • They respond best to "touch more, talk less" and "act don't yak" approaches — kills C
  • Some situations are more likely to trigger symptoms than others, and the ability to concentrate on fun or interesting tasks does not exclude the diagnosis — kills D

flags.title: Orphaned vignette
flags.html: "Bill" is never introduced anywhere in this section. Q42 is a general ADHD question with no patient. The case that presumably introduced Bill has been lost from the section, but Q43 and Q44 are still answerable as general ADHD management questions.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q42-Q44. Tests [[07 - Approach to ADHD]].
stem: After a careful discussion of risks and benefits, you start Bill on Ritalin (methylphenidate). His parents have brought him back to your office one week later with concerns that the medication is "not working". Of the following, what would be the MOST reasonable next step?

options.html: Start Adderall (amphetamine) while also continuing Ritalin.
Start Strattera (atomoxetine) while also continuing Ritalin
Counsel the parents that it takes several weeks for stimulants to have a therapeutic effect.
Stop all medications, because failure to respond to a first line stimulant means that Bill will be resistant to pharmacological treatment.

answer:
The correct answer is B. Four rules settle it:

  • Stimulants usually begin to act immediately — so C is wrong, and one week is long enough to judge
  • It is never appropriate to combine stimulants — so A is wrong (methylphenidate + amphetamine)
  • The non-stimulant Strattera MAY be combined with ONE stimulant medication ✓
  • Both of these are first-line treatments, and it may be necessary to try several — so D is wrong

Catapres is a second-line treatment and would not be used until several other treatments had failed — so E is premature.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q49-Q50. Tests [[09 - Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities]].
stem: Which of the following is TRUE about autism?

options.html: Males are more commonly affected than females.
Autism and mental delay rarely occur together.
Patients with autism tend to have a smaller head circumference than controls.
Most patients with autism have a known chromosomal abnormality.

answer: The correct answer is A — males are more commonly affected than females. The distractors: intellectual disability commonly co-occurs (B); head circumference tends to be larger, not smaller (C); most patients have no identified chromosomal abnormality (D); and autism is not caused by vaccines (E). See autism spectrum disorder.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q49-Q50. Tests [[09 - Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities]].
stem: Roy is a 6-year-old boy who is brought to your office by his parents, who are concerned about his development. They note that he has abnormally intense interests. For example, he knows the location of every tornado in the past 20 years. He also exhibits flapping of his hands and is preoccupied with parts of objects. He has few close relationships and prefers to play alone. However, his language development has been normal and there are no signs of cognitive impairment. What would be the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: More information needed to make the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder

answer:
The correct answer is E. The presentation describes what used to be called Asperger's Syndrome — but that is no longer a part of the DSM, which is why B is not available as an answer.

And ASD itself cannot yet be diagnosed: some of Roy's behaviours suggest ASD, but we don't know how early in development this started, and we don't know whether he satisfies the 3 social interaction/communication criteria and the 2 repetitive behaviour criteria required for the diagnosis. This case is best dealt with by further ASD screening questions.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q97-Q98. Tests [[08 - Speech and Language Disorders]].
stem: A 10-year-old boy presents to the clinic with a history of struggling in school. He has difficulty with reading and writing, often misspelling words and having difficulty with sentence structure. He also struggles with math concepts and has difficulty with basic calculations. He has had difficulty keeping up with his peers academically and has been receiving tutoring for several months. His teacher reports that he is easily distracted and has difficulty following instructions. He has no significant medical history. What type of learning disorder is most likely affecting this patient?
answer:
The workbook's answer is C — dyscalculia, on the reasoning that difficulty with math concepts and basic calculations is consistent with dyscalculia. The definitions:

  • Dyslexia — difficulty with reading and writing
  • Dysgraphia — difficulty with handwriting and written expression
  • Dyscalculia — difficulty with mathematics
  • ADHD — a neurodevelopmental disorder of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, not a learning disorder

flags.title: The stem describes all three learning disorders at once
flags.html: The boy has difficulty with reading and spelling (dyslexia), sentence structure (dysgraphia) and math (dyscalculia), plus distractibility and difficulty following instructions. Nothing in the stem singles out the math difficulty as primary, so the letter is not well supported — a mixed learning disorder with possible comorbid ADHD is the more honest reading. The definitions above are the durable content; do not over-invest in the letter.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q97-Q98. Tests [[08 - Speech and Language Disorders]].
stem: Continuation of Question 97: Which of the following interventions is most appropriate for this patient?

options.html: Educational interventions, such as individualized tutoring or specialized education services
Referral to a neurologist for further testing

answer:
The correct answer is C. Educational interventions — individualized tutoring or specialized education services — are the first-line intervention for learning disorders, and may include teaching strategies and accommodations.

Why the others are not first line:

  • Stimulant medication treats ADHD symptoms, not learning disorders
  • Psychotherapy may help with emotional or behavioural issues related to the learning disorder
  • Neurology referral is considered only if there is concern for an underlying neurological condition

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35-Q37, Q45-Q46. Tests [[10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders]].
stem: Andy is a 12-year-old boy who has been brought to you for an evaluation because he has been refusing to attend school. Which of the following is TRUE about conducting the initial interview?

options.html: If Andy's parents have a good relationship with him, taking time to speak with Andy alone will be counterproductive.
You should try to relate to Andy as if you were an older sibling, because this will put him at ease.
You may need to spend extra time building rapport, as it was not Andy's idea to come to see you.
You can probably get a full understanding of the situation from Andy and his parents, so it will not be necessary to speak to anyone at Andy's school.
Because Andy is only 12, anything that he says to you can be repeated to his parents.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Four principles, each correcting one distractor:

  • Children want physicians who act as physicians — not as friends or siblings (kills B)
  • They are entitled to confidentiality and may have concerns to share with you alone (kills A and E)
  • You should gather collateral from every possible source (kills D)
  • You should be sensitive to the fact that the child may not wish to be there ✓

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35-Q37, Q45-Q46. Tests [[10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is the BEST approach to Andy's school avoidance?

options.html: Andy should be immediately hospitalized, as school avoidance is an extremely severe and uncommon symptom.
Andy should be homeschooled, as school is obviously not a healthy environment for him.
Andy should be treated for social anxiety, as this is the single major cause of school avoidance.
The best treatment for Andy will be returning to school, possibly with additional supports or a modified placement.
The parents should force Andy to return to school immediately – the reason behind his school avoidance is not important.

answer: The correct answer is D. School avoidance is a very common symptom with a wide variety of causes — which is what makes A ("uncommon") and C ("the single major cause") wrong. The best treatment for school avoidance is return to school with appropriate supports — which is what makes B (removal from school) and E (return without addressing the cause) wrong.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35-Q37, Q45-Q46. Tests [[10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following questions would it be MOST important to discuss privately with Andy's parents?

options.html: Have there been any arguments or conflicts with his siblings?
Is there any family history of suicide?
How does he get along with his peers?
Is there a history of developmental delay?

answer:
The correct answer is B. Discussion of developmental delay and family history of suicide are best saved for a private discussion, because they may be difficult for the child to understand, or may be something the family has not previously disclosed to the child.

E is the near-miss — it is on the same list of private topics, but family history of suicide is the more sensitive of the two, since it concerns information the child may not know at all.

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35-Q37, Q45-Q46. Tests [[10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders]].
stem: Mario is a 14-year-old boy who is brought to your office due to concerns regarding his behaviour. He is often hostile and defiant towards his mother, and will refuse to comply with even the simplest requests. He often loses his temper with his siblings, but does not engage in any criminal behaviour. Which of the following would be the BEST way to approach his condition?

options.html: Diagnose him with oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) and place him in a short term residential facility without attempting to modify his home environment.
Do not treat him, as he probably has antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), and therefore cannot be helped.
Perform a full psychiatric and medical assessment to screen for ADHD and other potential diagnoses which may be causing or exacerbating his behaviour.
Diagnose him with conduct disorder and tell his parents to call the police the next time he behaves defiantly towards them.
Advise his parents to withhold affection if he does not comply with rules.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Behavioural problems in teenagers may have a variety of sources and a full work-up is key. The specific exclusions:

  • ASPD cannot be diagnosed before the age of 18 — kills B
  • conduct disorder cannot be diagnosed without criminal behaviour, and the stem says he has none — kills D
  • ODD is a possible diagnosis, but if so, modification of the home environment and ongoing treatment would be key — kills A
  • Positive parenting and positive reinforcement are vital — kills E

weekLabel: Week 18 - Anxiety, OCD, Personality Disorders & Neurodevelopment
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35-Q37, Q45-Q46. Tests [[10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders]].
stem: If you were screening Mario for conduct disorder, which of the following is NOT one of the categories of behaviours which you would assess?
answer:
The correct answer is E. The four categories of conduct disorder behaviour are aggression to people or animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness/theft, and serious violation of rules.

Spiteful/vindictive behaviour is an ODD criterion, not a conduct disorder one — which is the distinction the question is drawing after Q45.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q9, Q30. Tests [[03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia]].
stem: The most common hallucination experienced in psychosis is?
answer: The correct answer is D. False sensory perceptions can occur in any modality — sight, smell, taste, touch or hearing — but auditory hallucinations are the most common in psychosis. Examples: hearing a running commentary (almost narration), hearing commands, and hearing thoughts out loud.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q9, Q30. Tests [[03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia]].
stem: An example of a negative symptom in psychosis is?

options.html: Believing the devil is trying to control them
Hearing a running commentary of their day

answer:
The correct answer is E. Negative symptoms reflect a loss of function: flat affect, poverty of thought, loss of interest in activities, and emotional and social withdrawal.

Positive symptoms are additions: delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder — and they may sometimes accompany mania.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q9, Q30. Tests [[03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia]].
stem: A man begins to complain about hearing voices weekly, but it only occurs right before he falls asleep. What is he experiencing?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Hypnagogic hallucinations are usually auditory but can be visual, tactile or other sensory events, are usually brief but occasionally prolonged, and occur at the transition from wakefulness to sleep.

If they occur going from sleep to wakefulness, it is hypnapompia. The mnemonic: hypnaGogic = Going to sleep. Neither is a psychotic phenomenon.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q9, Q30. Tests [[03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia]].
stem: A good prognosis predictor in schizophrenia includes?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Good prognostic predictors for schizophrenia: late onset, precipitating factors, acute onset, good pre-morbid function, mood disorder symptoms, married, family history of mood disorders, good support systems, and positive symptoms.

Every distractor is the inverse of an item on that list — family history of schizophrenia (not mood disorder), insidious onset, negative symptoms, early onset.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q9, Q30. Tests [[03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia]].
stem: MRI findings in Schizophrenia include which one of the following?

options.html: The correlation of temporal volume loss with negative symptoms
Gain of grey matter in the prefrontal cortex and cerebellum

answer:
The correct answer is A. On MRI, schizophrenia is associated with an increase in ventricular size, particularly in the temporal horns. Other findings:

  • widespread loss of grey matter — so C is the wrong direction
  • correlation of temporal volume loss with positive symptoms — so B has the symptom class wrong
  • frontotemporal connection anomalies — so D is wrong

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q18-Q19, Q31. Tests [[04 - Treatment of Psychotic Disorders]].
stem: Psycho-social treatment components for treating psychosis include all of the following except?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Exposure and response prevention is used to treat OCD, not psychosis. What each of the others contributes:

  • Skills development — social skills, vocational skills, stress management, to help daily functioning
  • Case management — coordination of care
  • Family psycho-education — helps the family understand the disorder and what to expect, and teaches coping strategies
  • CBT — reframing psychosis, identifying triggers, belief modification, disrupting symptoms

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q18-Q19, Q31. Tests [[04 - Treatment of Psychotic Disorders]].
stem: Which side effect of first-generation antipsychotic medications usually takes months to years to occur?
answer: The correct answer is E. Dystonia, parkinsonism and akathisia are all extrapyramidal symptoms and can be early-onset reactions. Tardive dyskinesia usually appears several years after the onset of medication — the word tardive means late. See antipsychotics.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q18-Q19, Q31. Tests [[04 - Treatment of Psychotic Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is true?

options.html: Typical antipsychotics effectively treat negative symptoms of psychosis
Tardive dyskinesia is more frequent with long term use of typical antipsychotics than atypical antipsychotics
Atypical antipsychotics have increased hyperprolactinemia compared to typicals

answer:
The correct answer is C. Tardive dyskinesia is more frequent with long-term use of typical antipsychotics than atypical ones.

Each distractor inverts a real fact:

  • A — typicals are poor at treating negative symptoms; that is a selling point of atypicals
  • B — haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic
  • D — clozapine lowers the seizure threshold
  • E — typicals cause more hyperprolactinemia than atypicals

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lecture: Consent, capacity & the Mental Health Act
lectureMeta: Workbook Q20, Q22. Tests [[05 - Consent, Capacity, and the Mental Health Act]]. Q22 refers to a "Mr. Howard" phone call the workbook **never prints** - the case is missing from the source, not from this transcription.
stem: Who can complete a Form 1?
answer: The correct answer is E — all of the above. Any physician may complete a Form 1 (Ontario Mental Health Act application for psychiatric assessment); it is not restricted to psychiatrists.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. See Q22 for the constraint that does apply.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lecture: Consent, capacity & the Mental Health Act
lectureMeta: Workbook Q20, Q22. Tests [[05 - Consent, Capacity, and the Mental Health Act]]. Q22 refers to a "Mr. Howard" phone call the workbook **never prints** - the case is missing from the source, not from this transcription.
stem: For the case above, after speaking with Mr. Howard on the phone, the family doctor decides the case sounds so severe that he is going to fill out the form 1 right away. He remembers when he saw Mrs. Howard 8 months ago at her checkup, and listening to what her husband described is so drastically different from how she appeared then, he feels certain that something is wrong. Since she won't seek help, he decides he needs to fill out a form 1 to ensure she at the very least has a psychiatric assessment. Why is he unable to do so?

options.html: A form 1 cannot be filled out for a patient suffering from a first episode
Mrs. Howard has to voluntarily consent to the form 1
Mrs. Howard does not seem to be at risk of harming herself or others
The physician must have seen the patient within the last 7 days
Mrs. Howard is suitable to be a voluntary patient

answer:
The correct answer is D. The physician must have personally examined the patient within the last 7 days to complete a Form 1. He last saw her 8 months ago — a phone call with her husband does not substitute.

Note that B is false as a general principle: a Form 1 is an involuntary assessment and does not require the patient's consent — that is the entire point of it.

flags.title: Orphaned vignette
flags.html: The stem opens "For the case above" — but there is no case above. The Howard vignette is not printed anywhere in this section; Q21 is about blood/injection phobias. The question is still answerable because the stem restates enough of the facts.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q38-Q40, Q99-Q100. Tests [[01 - Eating Disorders]].
stem: Toby is a 15-year-old boy who has been hospitalized for severe anorexia nervosa (75% IBW). Being an astute clinical clerk, you realize that you must monitor him for refeeding syndrome during his stay. Which of the following would be the BEST laboratory test to follow?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Refeeding syndrome occurs when rapid refeeding with carbohydrates following starvation generates large amounts of ATP, depleting the body's phosphate stores. It can cause unstable vitals, cardiac failure, pulmonary edema and death.

Monitoring schedule: phosphate daily × 5, then every 2 days × 3 weeks, and supplement if necessary.

The other labs matter but for a different reason: they are important to follow and may provide an indication for hospitalization (K < 3, USG < 1.01 or > 1.03) — but they are not associated with refeeding syndrome.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q38-Q40, Q99-Q100. Tests [[01 - Eating Disorders]].
stem: Eve is a 14-year-old girl who is brought to your office by her parents due to concerns over her rapid weight loss. When you weigh her, you discover that she currently weighs 80% of her ideal body weight (IBW). Her last menstrual period was two months ago. Her parents report that she will eat a normal amount of food at meal times, but shortly afterwards will run to the bathroom and lock herself inside for up to half an hour. Eve admits that she sometimes causes herself to throw up after she eats, but states that she is "the size of an elephant" and will do anything to avoid gaining weight. Which of the following EXCLUDES the diagnosis of anorexia nervosa?

options.html: Eve continues to eat normal-sized meals with the rest of her family.
Eve's weight is more than 75% of her Ideal Body Weight (IBW)
Eve's last menstrual period was 2 months ago.
Eve is cooperative and willing to admit that she has been causing herself to vomit after meals.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Weight > 75% IBW excludes it, on the workbook's threshold. Per the DSM-5 a patient must have significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory and physical health.

Each distractor is a non-exclusion:

  • A and B — patients may restrict (restricting subtype) or binge and purge (binge/purge subtype), so purging is compatible with anorexia nervosa
  • E — cooperativity does not affect diagnosis (though it is often poor)

Compare Q40, where the same 75% threshold is used in the other direction.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q38-Q40, Q99-Q100. Tests [[01 - Eating Disorders]].
stem: Elisa is a 13-year-old girl who is brought to you by her parents regarding concerns of weight loss. On history, Elisa reports that she has periods of several hours during which she will eat "anything that is in front of her" without any ability to control how much she is eating. These have been occurring 2-3 times per week for the past 6 months. She reports that after one of these episodes, she will "diet" for several days, usually eating only 1-2 salads. Upon further questioning, she states that a salad consists of four baby carrots, a stick of celery, and four lettuce leaves, with no dressing. She denies any history of vomiting or laxative or diet pill abuse. Her weight is currently 90% of her IBW and she states that this makes her happy, as she will do anything to avoid "getting fat". What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis at this time?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Two exclusions in sequence:

  • Not anorexia: BN is distinguished from AN because AN patients have a body weight < 75% IBW — Elisa is at 90%. (Both AN and BN patients place excessive value on weight and may or may not purge.)
  • Not binge eating disorder: BN patients engage in compensatory behaviours — and restricting is an example of a non-purging compensatory behaviour. Her multi-day near-starvation "diets" after each binge are the compensation.

She denies vomiting, laxatives and diet pills, so it is the non-purging subtype.

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q38-Q40, Q99-Q100. Tests [[01 - Eating Disorders]].
stem: A 17-year-old female presents to the clinic with a concern for weight loss. She has lost approximately 20 pounds over the past three months, and reports restricting her caloric intake to less than 800 calories per day. She reports feeling guilty or ashamed after eating, and denies any episodes of binge eating or purging. She reports an intense fear of gaining weight, and reports feeling fat despite being underweight. She reports missing her menstrual period for the past three months. She denies any significant medical history. What is the most likely differential diagnosis for this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Significant weight loss, restriction of caloric intake, intense fear of gaining weight and distorted body image are consistent with anorexia nervosa, restricting type.

The three exclusions, each turning on one absent feature:

  • BN requires recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behaviours — she denies both
  • BED requires recurrent binge eating without compensation — she denies bingeing
  • ARFID is avoidance or restriction of food intake without the body image distortion — and she has marked body image distortion

weekLabel: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law
lectureMeta: Workbook Q38-Q40, Q99-Q100. Tests [[01 - Eating Disorders]].
stem: In the patient from question 99, which of the following is a potential medical complication associated with this condition?
answer:
The workbook's answer is A — amenorrhea, a common complication of anorexia nervosa due to low body weight and caloric restriction. Other complications: bradycardia, electrolyte imbalances, osteoporosis.

C and D are the true exclusions: hypertension is not typically associated with anorexia (it may be seen in some patients with binge eating disorder or bulimia nervosa), and hyperthyroidism is not associated either.

flags.title: Two options are both correct
flags.html: The key's own explanation states that "bradycardia... may also be present in patients with anorexia nervosa due to the effects of malnutrition on the cardiovascular system" — so B is equally a potential complication, and the question as written has two right answers. A is presumably intended because the stem already mentions three months of amenorrhea.

weekLabel: Week 20 - Sleep, Boundaries, Delirium & Cognitive Disorders
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q53, Q90. Tests [[01 - Sleep Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following is TRUE about REM sleep?

options.html: REM sleep mostly occurs in the first half of the sleep period
Any dreams that are experienced will likely be concrete and realistic.
Due to skeletal muscle paralysis, it is unlikely to have an erection during REM sleep
REM sleep is a poikilothermic state

answer:
The correct answer is E. REM sleep is a poikilothermic state — thermoregulation is suspended. Every other option is false:

  • A — the extraocular muscles are active (hence rapid eye movement)
  • B — REM tends to occur in the second half of the sleep period
  • C — dreams tend to be surreal and abstract, not concrete and realistic
  • D — penile erection does occur during REM

weekLabel: Week 20 - Sleep, Boundaries, Delirium & Cognitive Disorders
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q53, Q90. Tests [[01 - Sleep Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following most often occurs during REM sleep?
answer: The correct answer is E (A and C). Sleep walking and sleep terrors typically occur during non-REM sleep, which excludes B and D. Nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out complex or violent behaviours) are the REM parasomnias.

weekLabel: Week 20 - Sleep, Boundaries, Delirium & Cognitive Disorders
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q53, Q90. Tests [[01 - Sleep Disorders]].
stem: Which of the following represents a parasomnia:
answer: The correct answer is D. Parasomnias are abnormal activities during sleep — sleep terrors, sleep walking and the like. The other options are all dyssomnias, which are disorders of the amount, quality or timing of sleep — insomnia, hypersomnia, narcolepsy, circadian rhythm disorders.

weekLabel: Week 20 - Sleep, Boundaries, Delirium & Cognitive Disorders
lectureMeta: Workbook Q47-Q48. Tests [[03 - Maintaining Boundaries]].
stem: Which of the following is MOST likely to be a boundary violation as opposed to a boundary crossing?

options.html: Accepting a small Christmas gift from a patient you have treated for five years.
Asking a patient if it would be okay to hug them when they are experiencing a particularly difficult time.
Replying to a patient who asks you if you have children, who feels very anxious about whether you can relate to their struggles as a parent.
Calling a patient during your vacation because you feel anxious and need to reassure yourself that they are okay.
Giving a pillow from your office to a patient who is insecure and feels comforted by holding something that you have touched.

answer:
The correct answer is D. The principle: accepting or giving small gifts, allowing some physical comforting (with the patient's explicit permission) and replying to questions may all be appropriate in certain contexts — these are crossings. Actions taken for the benefit of the clinician — such as calling a patient because of your own anxiety — are violations, because they are not done in the patient's best interests.

The three things to weigh: the context of the action, the consistency of your behaviour across patients, and for whose benefit the action is undertaken.

flags.title: The key inverts both definitions
flags.html: The key states: "Boundary violations are deviations from traditional therapeutic activities that are harmless or even enhance the therapy" — that is the definition of a crossing. And it concludes: "Actions taken for the benefit of the clinician... are boundary crossings" — that is a violation. The two terms are swapped throughout the explanation, even though the letter D is correct. The version above restores the correct usage.

stem: Gloria is a patient in your family practice who presents to your office complaining of symptoms of an STI. Upon further questioning, you discover that she has been seeing a psychologist for psychotherapy, and that the two are involved in a sexual relationship. She asks you not to tell anybody, as she feels that the relationship is consensual. Which of the following is TRUE about your obligations under the Regulated Health Professionals Act (RHPA)?

options.html: Since psychologists are not members of the CPSO, you have no responsibility to file a report.
You may not file a report without Gloria's consent, as confidentiality is always your primary obligation.
You must file a report, but Gloria may refuse to have her name included, in which case the report will not be acted upon.
You may face disciplinary action if you wait longer than 3 months before filing a report.
If the psychologist were to terminate treatment with Gloria and refer her to another psychotherapist, it would be appropriate for them to continue a sexual relationship.

answer:
The correct answer is C. The rules:

  • You are required to file a report within 30 days of learning that a member of any regulated profession has been sexually involved with a patient — which kills A (any regulated profession, not just CPSO members) and D (30 days, not 3 months)
  • You must file whether or not the patient consents — which kills B
  • But you may only name the patient with their consent, and without a name the report will not be acted upon ✓
  • Conducting a sexual relationship with a former psychotherapy patient is never appropriate, no matter how much time has elapsed — which kills E

lectureMeta: Workbook Q16-Q17, Q75. Tests [[04 - Delirium]].
stem: Mr. Jones is a 74-year-old man who has been in the hospital for two weeks. All of a sudden, he has impaired memory and judgement, clouding of consciousness, and disorientation. He also seems to be hearing things that are not there. He gets better and worse throughout the day and is worse at night. What is Mr. Jones suffering from?
answer:
The correct answer is D. 30-40% of hospitalized patients over 65 have at least one episode of delirium — Mr. Jones is 74 and two weeks into an admission.

The two features that differentiate it from dementia are the acute onset and the clouding of consciousness. The impaired memory, disorientation and perceptual disturbances all fit, as does the fluctuating course that is worse at night.

answer: The correct answer is A. All of the listed factors are risk factors for delirium, but age is the most widely identified one.

stem: Jim is a 75-year-old male who is brought to the emergency department by police after being found wandering around the park in a confused state, believing that he is on a special mission from God. Which of the following is the LEAST likely explanation for his presentation?

options.html: Mania secondary to a physical condition
First onset of classical Bipolar I disorder.

answer: The correct answer is E. Bipolar I disorder usually onsets in early adulthood. A first episode of manic symptoms in an elderly adult is more likely to be due to a substance or a general medical condition — which is precisely what options A, B, C and D offer.

stem: Which of the following is false?

options.html: Neurocognitive Disorder (NCD) has normal general cognitive function and activities of daily living
People with MCI will all go on to dementia, most within 5 years
There is no current proven treatment for NCD
Other common causes of mild memory loss need to be ruled out, before a diagnosis of NCD can be made
Chronic exposure to anticholinergics is a common (and reversible) cause of NCD in the elderly

answer: The correct answer is B. Only 20-40% of people with MCI go on to dementia — not all of them. The word "all" is what makes the statement false.

stem: The most common cause of dementia in Canada is?
answer: The correct answer is A — Alzheimer's type.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. Note that B (mixed) is the substantial distractor, since mixed pathology is very common at autopsy — but pure Alzheimer type remains the most common clinical diagnosis.

stem: Mrs. Stanley comes to see you at your office. She says she is concerned because her mother was just diagnosed with dementia and she is worried that she will end up with dementia as well. She is 55 years old and lives at home with her husband and youngest child, her elder two are at university. She is currently employed as a lawyer and went to law school at Western. She doesn't drink and has smoked for the last 30 years. She is currently taking medication to control her blood pressure and cholesterol as well as estrogen supplementation to help with her menopause symptoms. Which one of her dementia risk factors is protective?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Greater education — along with continued mental, physical and social stimulation — is a protective factor. Law school gives her 18 years.

Note the question's phrasing: it asks which of her risk factors is protective, i.e. which item in her history moves the risk down rather than up. Smoking and hypertension raise risk; abstinence and estrogen supplementation are not protective.

stem: Jerry is an 85-year-old male who is brought to your office by his wife, who has noticed that he is experiencing increased difficulty with his memory and cognition. She also notes that he no longer enjoys his hobbies the way that he used to. Which of the following is the MOST convincing evidence that Jerry's cognitive impairment is due to dementia as opposed to his major depressive episode?

options.html: During the word recall task, Jerry is unable to recall the word "apple", but remembers it when you tell him "the word is a type of fruit".
Jerry has decreased attention and concentration, but he is oriented to place, time, and person.
When Jerry misplaces his reading glasses, he feels convinced that his neighbour has stolen them.
Jerry is unable to write his name on a piece of paper.
Jerry tells you that he doesn't feel sad at all, and that he doesn't understand why his wife thinks he is depressed.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Cognitive impairment due to dementia is characterized by loss of orientation, no response to cueing, and impairment of higher functions — agnosia, apraxia, agraphia. Inability to write his name is agraphia.

Each distractor points away from dementia or is non-discriminating:

  • A — responding to a cue ("a type of fruit") suggests a retrieval deficit, which favours depression
  • B — preserved orientation argues against dementia
  • C and E — elderly patients often deny a depressed mood but may report lack of interest in activities and delusional symptoms, so both are compatible with depression

weekLabel: Week 20 - Sleep, Boundaries, Delirium & Cognitive Disorders

stem: Upon further questioning, Jerry reports that he has experienced frequent headaches, dizziness, and back pain for around 6 months, which his family doctor is unable to explain. Which of the following is CORRECT regarding treatment of Jerry's depression?

options.html: Cipralex (escitalopram) would be a good choice of antidepressant due to its particular efficacy in treating pain and somatic symptoms.
There would be an increased risk of lithium toxicity at a standard dose due to the decrease in hepatic function that occurs with aging.
Seroquel (quetiapine) would be a safe choice for Jerry due to low risk of cerebrovascular complications.
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a safe and effective option for the treatment of depression in the elderly.
Elavil (amitriptyline) would be a good choice of antidepressant due to its particular efficacy in treating pain and somatic symptoms.

answer:
The correct answer is D. ECT is a safe and effective option in the elderly and may be preferable to medication in patients who are already on multiple medications or whose condition is fragile.

Each distractor:

  • A — SSRIs are not indicated for somatic symptoms; the good choice for that would be Cymbalta (duloxetine)
  • B — there would be increased risk of lithium toxicity, but due to impaired renal function — lithium is not handled by the liver
  • C — atypical antipsychotics are risky in the elderly due to increased risk of cerebrovascular disease, so quetiapine is the opposite of safe here
  • E — TCAs are effective for pain and somatization, but their anticholinergic side effects make amitriptyline a poor choice in an 85-year-old

stem: Which of the following dementias show significant improvement in cognition, behaviors and function with cholinesterase inhibitors? (Select all that apply)
answer:
The correct answers are A, B, E. Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) are approved for:

  • Alzheimer's
  • Lewy body dementia
  • Mixed dementia (Alzheimer's + vascular)

They are NOT approved for frontotemporal or vascular dementia — note the asymmetry that mixed Alzheimer's/vascular qualifies while pure vascular does not.
